questiontext.text: In a B-tree of order m, how many keys and children can a single node hold at most?

answer.text: Up to m−1 keys and up to m children

feedback.text: Correct — a node with k keys has k+1 children, so at most m−1 keys and m children.

answer.text: Up to m keys and up to m−1 children

feedback.text: Reversed — keys are one fewer than children.

answer.text: Exactly 2 keys and 3 children

feedback.text: That describes only a 2-3 tree (order 3), not the general case.

answer.text: Up to m keys and up to m children

feedback.text: Children always exceed keys by exactly one.

generalfeedback.text: Order m bounds a node to m−1 keys; the separating keys create m child pointers.

questiontext.text: What is true about the leaves of a B-tree?

answer.text: All leaves lie at the same depth

feedback.text: Correct — the B-tree stays perfectly height-balanced.

answer.text: Leaves may differ in depth by up to one level

feedback.text: No — every leaf is at exactly the same depth.

answer.text: Only the leftmost path reaches a leaf

feedback.text: Every root-to-leaf path has equal length.

answer.text: Leaves store no keys, only child pointers

feedback.text: In a B-tree leaves do store keys.

generalfeedback.text: Insertions grow the tree by splitting upward, so all leaves always remain equidistant from the root.

questiontext.text: Why is a B-tree preferred over a binary search tree for disk-resident data?

answer.text: High fan-out gives low height, so a search touches few nodes and few disk/block reads

feedback.text: Correct — each node maps to a disk block; fewer levels mean fewer I/O operations.

answer.text: It stores every key in RAM so no disk is needed

feedback.text: B-trees are designed precisely for data too large for RAM.

answer.text: It compresses keys to save disk space

feedback.text: The motivation is reducing I/O count, not compression.

answer.text: It sorts data faster than quicksort

feedback.text: It is a search structure, not a sorting algorithm.

generalfeedback.text: A disk seek is far costlier than a comparison; wide nodes minimize the number of blocks read per query.

questiontext.text: What is the time complexity of search, insert, and delete in a B-tree with n keys?

answer.text: O(log n)

feedback.text: Correct — the balanced height is logarithmic in n.

answer.text: O(n)

feedback.text: That would be a degenerate list, which B-trees avoid by balancing.
You still descend a logarithmic number of levels.

answer.text: O(n log n)

feedback.text: That is a total sorting cost, not a single operation.

generalfeedback.text: Balanced height guarantees logarithmic search, insert, and delete.

questiontext.text: In a classic B-tree, keys (and their associated data) are stored in both internal and leaf nodes.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — unlike a B+ tree, a B-tree keeps data in internal nodes too.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: A B-tree stores keys throughout; only the B+ tree confines data to leaves.

questiontext.text: Every non-root node of a B-tree of order m must hold at least ⌈m/2⌉−1 keys.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — this minimum-occupancy rule keeps the tree at least half full and balanced.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The lower bound ⌈m/2⌉−1 is exactly what guarantees balance.

questiontext.text: A B-tree is a balanced multiway search tree because all of its ______ lie at the same depth. (one word)

answer.text: leaves

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: leaf

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: leaves*

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about B-trees are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Node occupancy is kept between ⌈m/2⌉−1 and m−1 keys

feedback.text: Yes — this bounded fill keeps the structure balanced.

answer.text: They are designed to minimize disk/block accesses

feedback.text: Yes — low height means few I/O operations.

answer.text: They confine all data to the leaves and link the leaves together

feedback.text: No — that describes a B+ tree, not a B-tree.

answer.text: Each node has at most two children

feedback.text: No — that is a binary tree; a B-tree node has up to m children.

generalfeedback.text: B-trees keep bounded occupancy for balance and wide nodes for low-I/O search; leaf-only data with linked leaves is the B+ tree.
